Title: BPF Token Delegation
Description:
What Is a BPF Token? The BPF Token prevents a process from gaining full root-level access to execute BPF code. The kernel hands out a BPF Token as a special permission slip to run BPF code. Only the privileged process can provide these specific BPF permissions, like loading, creating maps, etc to an unprivileged one to execute code or create maps, etc. Kernel version 6.9 introduced the BPF Token.
Why Do I Want To Hand-Roll a BPF Token Delegation? Anywhere I searched for “BPF tokens”, I kept getting something like, “BPF tokens let unprivileged containers load eBPF" and I wanted to use it, but all Google searches either led me to kernel commit messages or nearly 100% AI generated blog posts. When I read these blog posts, they didn’t make sense, and I couldn’t find examples of failures someone ran into, or an explanation of why doing it a certain way led to failure, which IMO is critical to understanding the internals.

Title: Lost in translation: What I learned trying to speedrun subtitles with LLMs
Description:
Several months ago, a good friend of mine, who knows I’m into birdwatching, suggested I watch a YouTube documentary called LISTERS: A Glimpse Into Extreme Birdwatching. Little did I know at the time that it would consume much of my free time and prevent me from blogging with my usual cadence!
I’ll say it right away: the documentary is one of the best I’ve seen. I was blown away by the storytelling, the camera work, the silly jokes and the overall quality of the movie that two guys from St. Louis were able to put together. And once they were done, they just posted it on YouTube. No fanfare, no proper distribution, no deals. In fact, I was so smitten by how good it was that I decided I needed to watch it with someone special in my life.

Title: A Little Less Software Clutter
Description:
I am obsessed with decluttering.
Not just with having fewer things, but with reducing the little traces things leave behind. Old folders. Duplicate versions. Applications that work, technically, but have no proper place in the system. I like things to be clear and minimal. Sometimes that instinct helps me. Sometimes it hurts. For now, it is what it is.
Linux portable apps are a good example. A .tar.gz file is easy to download, but afterward I am left deciding where it belongs, how to launch it, how to update it, and how to remove it without leaving pieces behind.

Title: Building a mini Homelab that fits in my carry-on
Description:
I'm traveling to Chicago for VCF Midwest next month. I'll be demoing NTP time history on vintage Macs, with my own GPS-derived NTP service hosted on an Xserve G5, synced via NTP or a strange AppleTalk timing extension from the 1990s.
So I built a little 'portable homelab' (pictured above) that supports 1-10 Gbps networking, can run off a small battery for at least an hour, switches between multiple WANs (so I can get my own 5G Internet connection, in case I need it), and gives me 12 wired Ethernet connections.

Title: Don't Let LLMs Play Telephone With Your Ideas
Description:
A prompt is for communicating an idea to an LLM.
If you tell your idea to an AI agent and ask it to write down in its own words, say, a “skill” document which is meant to be a reusable piece of prompt to attach to another LLM session, it becomes a classic game of telephone. The model inevitably misinterprets your unspoken context or invent its own rules that you never intended. So the process is guaranteed to be lossy, therefore worse than your original words.
